title: Low-level environmental lead exposure in childhood and adult intellectual function: a follow-up study.
ehr_evidence: We recruited adults in the Boston area who had participated as newborns and young children in a prospective cohort study that examined the relationship between lead exposure and childhood intellectual function.
summary: Follow-up study assessing the relationship between early-life environmental lead exposure and adult intellectual function in a prospective cohort.
key_findings: Childhood blood-lead concentration (mean of ages 4 and 10) had the strongest relationship with Full-Scale IQ (b = -1.89 ± 0.70, p = 0.01).
Full-scale IQ was significantly related to blood-lead concentration at age 6 months (b = -1.66 ± 0.75, p = 0.03), 4 years (b = -0.90 ± 0.41, p = 0.03), and 10 years (b = -1.95 ± 0.80, p = 0.02).
Adjusting for maternal IQ altered the significance of the regression coefficient for blood lead.
captured_features: blood lead concentrations at multiple time points
population: adults aged 28-30 years (n=43) originally enrolled as newborns in a Boston cohort (1979-1981)
limitations: limited ability to perform multivariate analysis
potential confounding by maternal IQ cannot be excluded
